title: Right Livelihood: Two Lists
hookLine: right livelihood in a modern job: what harm does it do, what good
carry: right livelihood: what you sell and how you sell
tomorrow: is it ever right to stop pushing so hard?

lines: A SECOND LIST: HOW YOU DEAL.
cards: A job listing says fast-paced environment and competitive pay, and everyone knows to read between the lines. Here's an older list that reads oddly too.
The Buddha names five trades a lay follower shouldn't deal in: weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants and poison. That's it. No list of jobs, no never be this or that.

Trades. And elsewhere, when he describes wrong livelihood, the list isn't about products at all. It's about how people deal: scheming, talking things up, hinting, belittling, using gain to chase more gain.
So which is it? What you sell, or how you sell it?

teach.b: The answer to the puzzle is: both. The two lists look at the same thing from two sides.

The first asks what passes through your hands, and whether it harms by its nature: things made to wound, people bought and sold, animals raised for slaughter, things that cloud the mind, things made to kill.
The second asks how you deal, whatever you deal in. You can sell honest frames dishonestly.
Talking someone up so they'll buy, dropping hints, running down the shop across the street: the sutta counts that as wrong livelihood too.
Right livelihood, samma ajiva, is a factor of the eightfold path, alongside right speech and right action. So for a modern job, the question becomes two questions.

teach.h: WHAT HARM, WHAT GOOD, AND HOW?
teach.b: What harm does this work do, and what good? And how am I doing it? The teaching doesn't pretend any job is spotless.
It asks you to see clearly: know the harm, shrink it where you can, and grow the good. A nurse, a coder and a cashier can all ask the same two questions on a Monday morning.
Honest work isn't a job title. It's what you hand over, and how you hand it.

how: Right livelihood is a factor of the eightfold path; lay Buddhists weigh it when choosing work, and some avoid the five trades the Buddha named.

o: any job with a well-known, respected title
work that does good and is done without tricks
work that pays enough to give to charity

games.q: two lists, two sides — tap the pairs.
p: wrong livelihood in how you deal
what harm and good, and how?

s: right livelihood means only a few spiritual jobs are allowed
the five trades list is short; the rest is about harm, good, and how you deal.
the Buddha counts talking something up to make a sale as wrong livelihood
scheming, talking up, hinting and belittling are on the list.
if the product is harmless, how you sell it doesn't matter
the second list is all about how you deal, whatever you deal in.

games.q: you work at a phone store. your manager says to tell everyone the extended warranty is "basically required." what fits honest work?
o: offer it truthfully: what it covers, and that it's optional.
say it's required; the warranty itself is harmless, so it's fine.
never mention it, even to people who'd actually want it.
games.why: the warranty is harmless; "basically required" is the problem. honest work covers how you deal, not only what you sell.

practice: On a scrap of paper, draw a line down the middle. On one side write one harm your work or school day can do, even a small one; on the other, one good it does. Look at both, and circle the one you could tip a little.

wordCard.voice: Honest work: work that does more good than harm, done without scheming, flattery or tricks.

orig.note: Pali: samma ajiva, right livelihood, a factor of the eightfold path.

carryVoice: Your line: right livelihood, what you sell and how you sell it. That's two of fifty.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.177, Vanijja Sutta (five trades a lay follower should not engage in: weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants, poison)
Majjhima Nikaya 117, Mahacattarisaka Sutta (wrong livelihood: scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, pursuing gain with gain)
